title: Resistance and resistivity
summary: Explains electrical resistance, how it varies with conductor length and cross-sectional area, and introduces resistivity (rho) with typical values for common conductors.

sections.heading: Electrical resistance
paragraphs: The composition of a conductor determines the number of free electrons available for current flow. As electrons pass through a poor conductor they meet opposition, and this opposition is called resistance.
When a current of 1 A passes through a conductor with an emf of 1 V applied, the resistance is 1 ohm (1 Ω).
bullets: Resistance is the opposition to electron flow

sections.heading: Resistance and length
paragraphs: A conductor can be thought of as a series of shorter lengths, like resistors in series, so total length and total resistance are both sums: LM = L1 + L2 + L3 + L4 and RT = R1 + R2 + R3 + R4. Resistance is proportional to length.
Worked example: a cable has a resistance of 0.15 Ω/m. For 320 m of the same cable, resistance = Ω/m × length = 0.15 × 320 = 48 Ω.

sections.heading: Resistance and cross-sectional area (csa)
paragraphs: Resistance is inversely proportional to the cross-sectional area. Doubling the csa halves the resistance, and halving the csa doubles it.

Worked example: 100 m of a conductor has a resistance of 0.076 Ω. With twice the csa the resistance is 0.076 × ½ = 0.038 Ω. With four times the csa it is 0.076 × ¼ = 0.019 Ω. With half the csa it is 0.076 × 2 = 0.152 Ω. With one quarter of the csa it is 0.076 × 4 = 0.304 Ω.
bullets: Resistance is inversely proportional to area
Twice the csa: 0.038 Ω; four times the csa: 0.019 Ω
Half the csa: 0.152 Ω; one quarter of the csa: 0.304 Ω

sections.heading: Resistivity
paragraphs: Resistivity is represented by the Greek letter ρ (rho). Its SI unit is the ohm metre (Ω⋅m), though the ohm centimetre (Ω⋅cm) is also used. If a 1 m × 1 m × 1 m solid cube of material has contacts on two opposite faces and 1 Ω between them, its resistivity is 1 Ω⋅m.
Any conductor has a specific resistance, also with the symbol ρ. It changes with temperature, so the temperature must be stated with it.
bullets: Resistivity at 20 °C: copper 1.72×10-8 Ωm, aluminium 2.65×10-8 Ωm
Other conductors: silver 1.59×10-8, gold 2.24×10-8, brass (58% copper) 5.90×10-8, brass (63% copper) 7.10×10-8 Ωm
R = conductor resistance in ohms; ρ = cable resistivity in Ωm; L = cable length in metres; A = cross sectional area in square metres

quiz.q: A cable has a resistance of 0.15 Ω/m. What is the resistance of 320 m of the same cable?
quiz.why: Resistance is proportional to length: 0.15 × 320 = 48 Ω.

quiz.q: 100 m of a conductor has a resistance of 0.076 Ω. What is the resistance of 100 m with twice the csa?
quiz.why: Resistance is inversely proportional to area, so 0.076 × ½ = 0.038 Ω.

quiz.q: 100 m of a conductor has a resistance of 0.076 Ω. What is the resistance of 100 m with half the csa?
quiz.why: Halving the csa doubles the resistance: 0.076 × 2 = 0.152 Ω.

quiz.q: 100 m of a conductor has a resistance of 0.076 Ω. What is the resistance with one quarter of the csa?
quiz.why: One quarter of the csa gives four times the resistance: 0.076 × 4 = 0.304 Ω.

quiz.q: How is resistance related to the cross-sectional area of a conductor?
quiz.why: Resistance is inversely proportional to area.
Resistivity is commonly represented by the Greek letter ρ (rho).

quiz.q: What is the SI unit of electrical resistivity?
quiz.why: The SI unit of electrical resistivity is the ohm metre (Ω⋅m).

quiz.q: Which of these conductors has the lowest resistivity at 20 °C?
quiz.why: Silver is 1.59×10-8 Ωm, lower than copper (1.72×10-8), gold (2.24×10-8) and aluminium (2.65×10-8).

quiz.q: What is the resistivity of copper at 20 °C?
Why must the temperature be stated when giving a conductor's specific resistance?
options: It is the same at all temperatures
quiz.why: Specific resistance changes with temperature, so the temperature must be stated.
